data.min_take_or_collateral_protection: YES — substantial, primary-source confirmed. AEP's new large-load/data-center tariffs include: (1) contract lengths of up to 20 years; (2) take-or-pay contractual minimums requiring a customer to pay for as much as 90% of contracted demand; and (3) cash or cash-related instruments as deposits/collateral (stated for both pending and approved tariffs). The OPCo "Ohio Data Center" tariff (PUCO, applying to new data-center load of 25 MW or more) is Approved. AEP frames these explicitly as protecting EXISTING customers and shifting build-out risk onto the large-load customer ("designed to protect existing customers... reduce risks around the build out of large load infrastructure on existing customers"). For ERCOT/AEP Texas, Texas SB 6 (effective June 2025) adds statutory protection to minimize stranded infrastructure costs and require large loads to pay a reasonable share of allocated transmission costs (rules being finalized through 2026). PJM-side, a Jan 2026 White House/13-governor Statement of Principles directs that costs of new capacity be paid by the large-load customers necessitating them. CAVEAT: the 36 GW AEP Texas figure is "Letters of Agreement" (non-binding LOAs), not executed take-or-pay contracts; and minimum-take/deposit terms protect against utility cost-of-service stranding but transmission/generation built ahead of ramp still carries timing and cancellation exposure (10-K explicitly warns an impairment "may need to be recorded in the event a project is canceled").
data.stranded_asset_risk_note: Moderate and explicitly disclosed. AEP's $72B 2026-2030 capital plan ($12.2B in 2026; $59.7B 2027-2030) is expressly driven by data-center/large-load growth (transmission + ~12,700 MW of new generation RFPs + 2.2 GW added in 2025 + up to 1 GW fuel-cell option). The structural mitigant is that most large-load cost is contracted to the AI/data-center customer via 20-year terms, up-to-90% take-or-pay minimums, and cash collateral/deposits — so if a data center cancels or leaves, the customer (not ratepayers) is contractually on the hook, materially reducing socialization/stranded-cost risk to existing ratepayers. Residual risks: (a) the 36 GW Texas figure is non-binding LOAs, not signed take-or-pay contracts, so the headline pipeline could shrink; (b) 10-K warns of impairment if a project is canceled and of execution risk (supply chain, capital-market access for capex exceeding historical financing needs); (c) generation/transmission built somewhat ahead of ramp; (d) regulatory risk that PUCs disallow imprudently incurred costs. Net: ratepayer protection is among the strongest in the sector due to PUCO/state-approved tariffs with high take-or-pay minimums, but it is contract-quality- and ramp-dependent, and a large share of the announced pipeline is still at LOA (non-binding) stage.

data.entity: Dominion Energy, Inc. (D) / Virginia Electric and Power Company ("Virginia Power" / Dominion Energy Virginia), CIK 0000715957
data.min_take_or_collateral_protection: PARTIAL / PHASING IN. As of FY2025, the principal protection was a firm-queue regime: deposits for expensive long-lead-time equipment plus reimbursement clauses for canceled projects, and "data center customer deposits" carried as restricted cash on the balance sheet (Note 2). The stronger, customer-specific protection is NOT yet in force: per the 2025 Biennial Review order, Virginia Power will BEGIN in JANUARY 2027 to require, for high-load (>=25 MW, >=75% load factor, including certain data centers) customers at connection: (1) a 14-year contract, (2) collateral over that 14-year period, and (3) demand minimums covering distribution, transmission AND generation revenues. The 10-K states these provisions are "designed to minimize both cross-rate class subsidies and stranded costs." Until Jan 2027 there is no system-wide 14-year minimum-take/collateral mandate, so pre-2027-connected data-center load and the bulk of the $55B generation/grid build are recovered through riders (rate adjustment clauses) and the rate base, i.e. socialized to all ratepayers, with the data-center minimum-take/collateral protection applying prospectively to new high-load connections.
data.stranded_asset_risk_note: Concentration risk is high and explicitly disclosed: data centers were 28% of Virginia Power's electricity sales in 2025 (26% in 2024), heavily concentrated in Loudoun County, VA, and PJM projects 5.4% average annual peak load growth for the DOM Zone over ten years. Virginia Power is building ~$55B of generation/grid (2026-2030, net of Stonepeak reimbursements) primarily to serve this load, including ~$8.3B dispatchable natural gas, the $1.5B/944 MW Chesterfield Energy Reliability Center gas plant (in service 2029), the $11.5B 2.6 GW CVOW offshore wind project, ~$6.9B solar, ~$2B storage, and ~$8.3B PJM-authorized transmission. Because most of this capital enters the rate base / is recovered via riders, a softening of AI/data-center demand or cancellation/relocation of hyperscaler load before the Jan-2027 14-year-contract/collateral regime takes hold would leave costs to be socialized across the remaining ~2.8M ratepayers (cross-subsidy and stranded-cost risk). Mitigants the 10-K cites: the firm-queue deposit/reimbursement requirements; data-center customer deposits held as restricted cash; the prospective Jan-2027 14-year contract + collateral + demand-minimum requirements; and for CVOW specifically, a 50% noncontrolling-interest sale to Stonepeak ($2.6B received) plus a Virginia Commission cost-sharing cap (recovery limited above $11.3B, no recovery $11.3B-$13.7B). Additional tail risk: Virginia's Retail Access Statutes allow certain large customers exceptions to Virginia Power's exclusive franchise, so high-load customers could potentially shop, eroding the load base backing the build.

data.stranded_asset_risk_note: CRITICAL STRUCTURAL POINT: NRG is a COMPETITIVE/MERCHANT independent power producer (IPP), not a rate-regulated vertically integrated utility. Its core ~12 GW (and the acquired ~13 GW LSP Portfolio) sit primarily in ERCOT/Texas and other deregulated markets that have NO traditional cost-of-service rate base. Therefore the classic Burry failure mode -- socializing AI-driven generation capex into a captive ratepayer rate base -- largely DOES NOT apply to NRG's own build. NRG owns and operates the new generation (Texas Development Projects: T.H. Wharton 415 MW peaker, Cedar Bayou 5 689 MW CCGT, Greens Bayou 6 443 MW peaker = ~1,547 MW; plus the GEV/Kiewit agreement for up to 5.4 GW of new gas CCGT and 3.6 GW of 7HA turbine slot reservations) and recovers it through merchant/contracted wholesale and retail revenues, so SHAREHOLDERS AND LENDERS bear the build/stranding risk -- NRG explicitly warns that if anticipated load growth fails to materialize it 'could incur additional expenses to terminate or redeploy any underutilized assets or infrastructure, or it may be unable to fully recover its capital expenditures.' PARTIAL SOCIALIZATION CHANNELS DO EXIST: (1) Texas Energy Fund (TEF) loans -- $216M (T.H. Wharton) + $562M (Cedar Bayou 5) + $370M (Greens Bayou 6) = $1.148B at a subsidized 3.0% fixed rate to 2045, plus PUCT completion-bonus grants -- are Texas taxpayer/state-subsidized financing for NRG-owned merchant plants, i.e. a public subsidy that shifts financing cost to Texas taxpayers even though the debt is recourse to NRG subsidiaries. (2) Generic ERCOT transmission cost allocation is under PUCT rulemaking (SB 6) and remains a socialization vector at the system level. STRANDED-ASSET RISK if AI demand softens: MATERIAL but borne mainly by NRG equity/debt, not captive ratepayers. NRG is committing ~7 GW+ of new gas generation against a Texas demand outlook (ERCOT peak 86 GW 2024 -> 139 GW 2030) that the 10-K itself flags as uncertain ('no assurance that these forecasts will be accurate'), with project delays/cancellations by data-center C&I customers named as a downside driver. (4) Blackstone JV gas plants in PA are to be built under long-term Energy Services Agreements (ESAs) with data-center developers/hyperscalers — i.e., customer-contracted, NOT rate-based — but as of the FY2025 10-K filing date "no ESAs with hyperscalers have been signed."
data.stranded_asset_risk_note: Stranded-asset risk is explicitly flagged by PPL itself and is REAL but currently bounded by the pre-contract/protected posture. The exposure is overwhelmingly PROSPECTIVE: PPL discloses NO contracted data-center MW and NO named hyperscaler customers, and states no hyperscaler ESAs were signed as of the FY2025 10-K. So the bubble-relevant capex is still optional/conditional, not committed-on-spec. Two distinct risk channels: (A) RATE-BASE channel (Kentucky regulated gas build): ~$3.7B of LG&E/KU generation (645 MW Brown Unit 12 NGCC, 645 MW Mill Creek Unit 6 NGCC, 400 MW/1,600 MWh BESS, Ghent Unit 2 SCR) approved by KPSC in Oct 2025 to serve "anticipated load growth, including from potential data center demand," recovered via rate-adjustment-clause mechanisms — i.e., RATEPAYERS bear this if data-center demand fails to materialize, though the Extremely High Load Factor Tariff (long-term contracts + minimum revenue payments + collateral) is the designed backstop. (B) CUSTOMER-CONTRACTED channel (PA Blackstone JV, PPL 51%/Blackstone 49%): gas plants built only against signed ESAs with hyperscalers, off the regulated rate base, so the JV/equity holders (and contracted hyperscalers via min-take) — NOT ratepayers — bear the risk; but the JV has already spent on land parcels with zero signed offtake. PPL's own risk factor: "If anticipated demand growth does not materialize, PPL could experience unrecovered capital investments." Net: ratepayer stranding risk is partially mitigated by special tariffs with minimum-bill/collateral terms, but the protection is only as strong as those (largely still-to-be-signed) contracts, and the Kentucky gas build proceeds into rate base ahead of firm data-center contracts.

corrections: Kentucky $3.7B build: the 10-K states KPSC EXCLUDED Brown Unit 12 and Mill Creek Unit 6 (the two 645 MW NGCC gas units, the bulk of the $3.7B) from the GCR/PGR rate-adjustment-clause recovery mechanism 'without prejudice to LG&E and KU seeking recovery of such costs in future proceedings' — so these dominant gas assets are NOT covered by the Extremely High Load Factor Tariff's minimum-revenue/collateral backstop and proceed toward traditional base-rate recovery (ratepayers).

The Extremely High Load Factor Tariff protects against future-customer default but does not ring-fence the gas capex itself; framing it as a backstop for the $3.7B build overstates ratepayer protection.

The 'customer-pays' (PA Blackstone JV ESA min-take) leg is entirely unsigned/prospective (no MW, no hyperscalers, no ESAs), and ESAs could be 'with the regulated utilities in Pennsylvania,' leaving open partial rate-base recovery — so it cannot be confirmed as a binding non-ratepayer allocation.
